title: A New Quantum Idea Starts With Very Unusual Helium
summary:
Static electricity can make your hair stick to a balloon. Small electrical disturbances can also cause trouble for a very different thing: a quantum computer.

These computers use units of information called qubits. Their information is delicate, and disturbances can introduce errors. Adding more qubits makes those errors harder to control.

Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a qubit using superfluid helium-3. A superfluid is a special liquid that can flow without friction. Their design uses helium with no electric charge, which could protect it from certain electrical disturbances.

The researchers' calculations suggest error rates could be about 100 times lower than those of conventional superconducting qubits. But that is a prediction, not a result from a finished device.

Lead author Priya Sharma says the next step is building a prototype and testing it. The design is called SHOQ.

It might eventually work alongside other quantum technology rather than replacing everything. One possible job is quantum memory: storing information while other equipment performs calculations. For now, the exciting part is an idea ready to face an experimental test.
why_it_matters: Errors are a challenge as quantum computers gain more qubits. This design proposes another way to protect information, but experiments must test its predictions.
